blocks.text: It is proved that כח coach is the ورل [waral] guaril, the largest and strongest of the lizards in Arabia.

Next comes כח coach, which almost all the ancients, as many as there are, place in the lizard family. The Greeks and Jerome render it chameleon. Both printed Arabic versions have حردون [ḥardūn] chardaun, that is, the land crocodile, or a species of it. So also R. Jonah and David Kimchi. R. Solomon has lizard. The Chaldee versions and the Samaritan keep the Hebrew word, with only the ending changed. But the Syriac, by a great error, has ܚܘܠܕܐ chulda here, and the manuscript Arabic versions الخلد [al-khuld] alchuld, that is, mole. Among the more recent translators, Pagninus, Münster, Castellio, the English and the Italians render it chameleon; Arias and Junius lizard; Petrus Robertus tortoise; Pomarius slug; certain Jews (in Gesner) squirrel; the Genevans crocodile. We side with those who understand a kind of lizard, because lizards are the subject here, and this is how most of the ancients take it, and the most ancient of them. Once this is granted, it will be easy to establish that the Hebrew name כח coach signifies الورل [al-waral], that is, the guaril of the Arabs, as the barbarous writers call it. This is clear from the name itself, which is taken from strength. For in more than a hundred other passages of Scripture כח coach is used for strength. And in Arabic كوح [kawḥ], with the same letters, means to be superior in a fight. It is therefore entirely fitting that, within the lizard family, the one called כח coach should be the one that is most powerful in strength and surpasses the rest in fighting. And that is undoubtedly الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or guaril, whose strength stands out above all in fighting against serpents and the land crocodile. Lest anyone call this into doubt, here are the most explicit testimonies of the Arabic writers on the matter! Alkazuini: هو عدو للضب وللحية يدخل بيتها وياكلها وليس شي من الحيوان اقوي علي قتل الحيات منه ولا يحتفر لنفسه بل يغتصب كل شي [II, 494] بيته لان اي بيت دخله هرب ساكنه وبغتصب بيت الحية كما يغتصب الحية بيت ساير الاجناس [huwa ʿaduww li-l-ḍabb wa-li-l-ḥayya yadkhulu baytahā wa-yaʾkuluhā wa-laysa shayʾ min al-ḥayawān aqwā ʿalā qatl al-ḥayyāt minhu wa-lā yaḥtafiru li-nafsihi bal yaghtaṣibu kull shayʾ baytahu li-anna ayy bayt dakhalahu haraba sākinuhu wa-byaghtaṣibu bayt al-ḥayya kamā yaghtaṣibu al-ḥayya bayt sāyir al-ajnās] It is hostile to the land crocodile and to the serpent, whose hiding place it enters in order to devour it. And no animal is stronger than it at killing serpents. [col. 1070] Nor does it dig a hiding place for itself, but it invades the hiding places of all others. For whatever hiding place it approaches, its occupant takes flight. Indeed, it invades the serpent's den, just as the serpent invades the dens of other kinds (I would prefer الاحناش ساير [sāyir al-aḥnāsh], of other reptiles). Algiahid on the same animal: وهو يقوي علي الحيات وياكلها اكلا ذريعا ويخرجها من حجرها ويسكن فيه فهو اظلم من ظالم [wa-huwa yaqwā ʿalā al-ḥayyāt wa-yaʾkuluhā aklan dharīʿan wa-yukhrijuhā min juḥrihā wa-yaskunu fīhi fa-huwa aẓlam min ẓālim] It prevails over serpents and eats them greedily, and drives them out of their hiding places in order to occupy them, and it is more violent than the violent. Abdollatif, followed by Damir: وبينه وبين الضب عداوة فيغلب الورل الضب ويقتله لكنه لا ياكله كما يفعل بالحيه وهو لا يتخذ بيتا لنفسه ولا يحفر حجرا بل يخرج الضب من حجره صارعا ويستولي عليه وانه كان اكثر براثن منه واقوي لكن الظلم يمنعه ولهذا يضرب به المثل في الظلم ويكفي في ظلمه انه يغصب الحية حجرها ويبلعها وربما قتل فوجد في بطنه الحية العظيمة وهو لا يتبلعها حتي يشدخ راسها [wa-baynahu wa-bayna al-ḍabb ʿadāwa fa-yaghlibu al-waral al-ḍabb wa-yaqtuluhu lākinnahu lā yaʾkuluhu kamā yafʿalu bi-l-ḥayya wa-huwa lā yattakhidhu baytan li-nafsihi wa-lā yaḥfiru juḥran bal yukhriju al-ḍabb min juḥrihi ṣāriʿan wa-yastawlī ʿalayhi wa-innahu kāna akthar barāthin minhu wa-aqwā lākin al-ẓulm yamnaʿuhu wa-li-hādhā yuḍrabu bihi al-mathal fī al-ẓulm wa-yakfī fī ẓulmihi annahu yaghṣibu al-ḥayya juḥrahā wa-yablaʿuhā wa-rubbamā qutila fa-wujida fī baṭnihi al-ḥayya al-ʿaẓīma wa-huwa lā yatabalaʿuhā ḥattā yashdakha raʾsahā] Between it and the τὸν [ton] dhab (or land crocodile) there is fierce enmity. But the guaril is superior and kills it. Yet it does not eat it, as it does with serpents. Nor does it choose a dwelling for itself or dig a hiding place. Rather, it thrusts the land crocodile out of its own home by wrestling, and prevails over it. Although the crocodile excels in the strength of its claws, this one is superior in violence. Hence its violence has become proverbial. It is so great in it that it suffices to thrust a serpent out of its den and devour it. Accordingly, a large serpent is sometimes found in the belly of one that has been killed; it does not swallow it without first crushing its head. There are many proverbs about it among the Arabs, of which these are worth noting: اجبر من الورل [ajbar min al-waral] Fiercer (or prouder) than the τῷ [tō] guaril. And اظلم من الورل [aẓlam min al-waral] More unjust (or more violent) than the τῷ [tō] guaril, to which Abdollatif alluded above. And اسرع من تلظم الورل [asraʿ min talaẓẓum al-waral] Quicker than the guaril turns food over in its mouth. To this belongs what Algiahid writes, that it eats the serpent greedily, or [II, 495] اكلا نريعا [aklan narīʿan], that is, literally, with a swift and headlong eating ^{(1)}. [col. 1071] From this description it appears that the name כח coach, taken from strength, suits this lizard exceedingly well ^{(2)}.
